meta.title: Who really said "It is only in order to shield your ignorance that you put the Lord at every turn to the refuge of a miracle"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Galileo. The sentence is in none of his works; its memorable phrase belongs to Thomas Browne, who used it of St Augustine, not of Galileo’s opponents.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is only in order to shield your ignorance that you put the Lord at every turn to the refuge of a miracle'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed to Galileo’s Dialogue by a 1955 biographer — but it is not in the Dialogue. “The refuge of a miracle” comes from Thomas Browne’s Religio Medici instead.

answer.label: Not Galileo — a sentence found in none of his works
answer.authorDates: Origin unidentified · in print by 1955, when Giorgio de Santillana pinned it on the Dialogue
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote lists this among Galileo’s misattributed quotations ↗, and the trail it gives is unusually specific: the historian Giorgio de Santillana attributed the remark to the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems in The Crime of Galileo (1955), “but it does not appear there.” The Fourth Day of the Dialogue does contain a vaguely similar exchange, where Salviati asks Simplicio why he reaches for a miracle to explain the tides. The sentence’s memorable phrase, however, is borrowed from somewhere else entirely: Thomas Browne’s Religio Medici ↗ is where someone is put “to the refuge of a miracle” — and the someone is St Augustine.

source.heading: Where the phrase really comes from

docMeta.dd: Galileo’s Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632) — where it does not appear
Giorgio de Santillana, The Crime of Galileo (1955)
Sir Thomas Browne, Religio Medici (first authorized edition, 1643)
St Augustine — the edition’s own note reads “St Augustine (De Civ. Dei, xvi. 7)”

source.excerpt: There is another secret, not contained in the Scripture, which is more hard to comprehend, and put the honest Father to the refuge of a miracle; and that is, not only how the distinct pieces of the world, and divided islands, should be first planted by men, but inhabited by tigers, panthers, and bears.
trail: Wikiquote’s Galileo page files the sentence under “Misattributed” ↗ with the finding that de Santillana attributed it to the Dialogue in 1955 “but it does not appear there,” and that “the specific wording comes instead from Thomas Browne’s Religio Medici.”

Browne’s sentence is in the Project Gutenberg text of Religio Medici ↗: a secret “more hard to comprehend” that “put the honest Father to the refuge of a miracle” — how tigers, panthers and bears reached islands after the Deluge. The same edition’s endnote identifies the Father: “St Augustine (De Civ. Dei, xvi. 7).”

That chapter is exactly the one Browne meant. City of God XVI.7 ↗ is headed “Whether Even the Remotest Islands Received Their Fauna from the Animals Which Were Preserved, Through the Deluge, in the Ark,” and among the possibilities Augustine weighs is that “it cannot be denied that by the intervention of angels they might be transferred by God’s order or permission.”

The same Wikiquote page shows what Galileo did write in this vein — “We seek not what God could have done but what He has done… God could have caused birds to fly with bones of solid gold… but He wanted to make their bones, flesh and feathers very light” — sourced there to notes in a copy of Jean-Baptiste Morin’s 1631 book on the earth’s motion ↗, and notes that English sources wrongly tack the “refuge of a miracle” sentence onto it.
source.excerptNote: The phrase in its original setting. Browne is not talking about astronomy or about anyone’s ignorance: he is puzzling over how predators reached remote islands after the Flood, and noting that the difficulty drove Augustine to invoke a miracle. The Gutenberg edition’s note on “the honest Father” reads, in full, “St Augustine (De Civ. Dei, xvi. 7).”

source.rightsNote: No rights status is asserted for the quoted sentence, because it has no identified author or first publication and cannot honestly be classified. Thomas Browne’s Religio Medici, the book the phrase comes from, dates from 1643 and is public domain — Project Gutenberg distributes it freely. Giorgio de Santillana’s The Crime of Galileo (1955), by contrast, remains in copyright.

author.metaLine: Origin unidentified · in circulation as Galileo by 1955
author.bio: The sentence is a composite with no traced author. Its rhetorical shape — accusing an opponent of hiding ignorance behind divine intervention — is a fair summary of an argument Galileo really made, and its most quotable phrase is lifted from a book by an English physician who was using it about St Augustine and the repopulation of islands after the Flood. Somewhere between the two, in English and probably in the twentieth century, a sentence formed that nobody wrote and everybody attributes.

misattribution.heading: A sentence assembled from other people’s
misattribution.intro: This is not a garbled Galileo line. It is a sentence with no original, whose most memorable words were written by an English doctor about a fifth-century bishop.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it among his misattributed quotations ↗: de Santillana placed it in the Dialogue in 1955, “but it does not appear there.” The nearest real exchange, on the Fourth Day, has Salviati asking Simplicio why he resorts to a miracle to explain the tides — a different question, in different words.

Browne writes that a difficulty “put the honest Father to the refuge of a miracle” — the passage is in the Gutenberg text ↗, and the “honest Father” is identified in the same edition’s notes as St Augustine, De Civ. Dei, xvi. 7 ↗. He supplies the phrase and nothing else; the rest of the sentence is not his.

items.who: Galileo, notes in a copy of Morin (1631)
items.tag: Genuine passage, not the source of this sentence
items.why: Wikiquote sources a real Galileo passage to those marginalia ↗: “We seek not what God could have done but what He has done… God could have caused birds to fly with bones of solid gold… but He wanted to make their bones, flesh and feathers very light.” The page notes that English sources wrongly finish that passage with the “refuge of a miracle” sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Galileo did think that appealing to miracles was a way of not doing physics, and he said so in his own words in the Morin marginalia. But the sentence people quote for it is not one of his ↗ — and the phrase that makes it quotable was coined by Thomas Browne, about the Flood.

context.heading: How a good paraphrase becomes a bad quotation
lead: The sentence is doing honest work. Galileo’s standing complaint against his Aristotelian opponents was that they explained away inconvenient results by appealing to what God could have arranged, rather than examining what He had. Reaching for a miracle whenever the mechanics ran out was, to him, a refusal to do the physics. A biographer summarising that in one sharp English sentence is not distorting him.

The trouble starts when the summary is set in quotation marks and given a page reference. Then it stops being a gloss and becomes evidence — and readers who go looking for it in the Dialogue find nothing, because there is nothing to find. The same page of Wikiquote that debunks this line also carries a second, cleaner version of the same error, with English sources appending the sentence to a genuine Galileo passage as though it were its conclusion.
context.detailsSummary: Browne, Augustine, and the tigers on the islands
detailsBody: Browne’s problem is zoological, not astronomical. Granted a universal Flood and a single ark landing on Ararat, how did tigers, panthers and bears end up on remote islands — and why does America teem with predators but lack horses? He calls it “another secret, not contained in the Scripture” ↗ and says it drove the honest Father to the refuge of a miracle.

Augustine had indeed been there. City of God XVI.7 ↗ weighs whether the beasts swam, whether men carried them for sport, and allows that “it cannot be denied that by the intervention of angels they might be transferred by God’s order or permission.” That is the refuge Browne means.

So the phrase arrives in the Galileo sentence carrying an argument about post-diluvian fauna, three centuries and one discipline away from the tides of the Dialogue. It is a good phrase. It was never about Galileo’s opponents.
context.pull: A fair summary of Galileo. Not a sentence of Galileo’s.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists this sentence under Galileo's Misattributed quotations, states that de Santillana attributed it to the Dialogue in The Crime of Galileo (1955) but that it does not appear there, and traces the wording to Thomas Browne's Religio Medici and City of God XVI.7.

Religio Medici contains "put the honest Father to the refuge of a miracle", about tigers, panthers and bears on divided islands after the Deluge, with the endnote "St Augustine (De Civ. Dei, xvi. 7)."

City of God XVI.7 is headed "Whether Even the Remotest Islands Received Their Fauna from the Animals Which Were Preserved, Through the Deluge, in the Ark" and concludes that angels might have transferred them by God's order or permission.
The Internet Archive holds a catalogue record for Giorgio de Santillana, The Crime of Galileo (1955).
Wikipedia gives Galileo's dates as 15 February 1564 – 8 January 1642.
Wikipedia gives Sir Thomas Browne's dates as 19 October 1605 – 19 October 1682.
